blocks.en: This cycle identified the cause of the repeated Luer valve breaks: KOH corroded the plastic. Only the valve on the KOH line was affected, so the rest of the data stands, and the next build needs alkaline-resistant Luer valves there. Tracing the breaks to a specific reagent on a specific line, rather than to the containment system, is also what lets us maintain the biosafety claim through a run that leaked twice.

blocks.en: The growth curve is the clean one the cycle was run to get: an exponential phase from about 2 to 9 hours and then a long slow climb to the end. The second exponential phase that appeared in cycle 5 does not appear here, and the difference between the two runs is that erythromycin was topped up with every morning feed. That settles a theory cycle 5 could only state: the second growth was the culture losing its selection, through contamination or through cells shedding the plasmid and the metabolic burden with it. It was not the vessel.

blocks.en: Holding pH at 7 improves bacterial growth and lets the culture reach a higher OD, which is the result this cycle set out to get. What it does not give is a protectant yield that climbs with it: the ELISA peaks at 12 hours and falls away, so a longer run is not a larger harvest, and raising output is a different problem from holding the vessel steady.

blocks.en: The loop as this cycle built it, and the version the machine ends on. Two servo-driven valves are new: the pinch valve on the culture return and the shell Luer valve on the protectant pathway. So is the dosing pump and its KOH bottle on the feeding valve.

blocks.en: The complete growth curve this cycle was run to get, with pH beneath it. The sawtooth in the lower panel is the dosing: each jump is base going in, and the decay between jumps is the culture acidifying the medium again. The first night is the automated controller working; the later, larger steps are the morning feeds after the dosing line was abandoned.

blocks.en: What a harvest does to the loop, second by second. In normal operation the peristaltic pump swings the transmembrane pressure between about −0.06 and +0.12 bar, so fluid crosses the membrane in both directions and the shell side never becomes dead volume. Closing the pinch valve lifts the whole oscillation above zero, which is the driving force for a harvest: the protectant only ever moves outward while the valve is shut.

blocks.en: The pinch valve, built to answer the gap Professor Chang named in June: the design had no driving force to move product across the membrane. Closing it raises the transmembrane pressure and pushes the permeate out.

blocks.en: The automated Luer valve on the shell side. It seals the opening from the lumen to the shell until a harvest is wanted, which is what lets the vessel keep its medium without anyone at the bench.

blocks.en: The vessel ran itself for three days on its own pH control. The thing that stopped it being unattended was not the biology or the electronics but a 20 cent plastic valve in the wrong material.

blocks.en: Show details The protein and activity time courses, and what three days of data settled about the harvest cycle.

blocks.en: Anti-His ELISA read the shell side at nine points to three days. ACC deaminase is present from the first hour, peaks at 12 hours and falls away: 4.80, 3.75, 6.52, 5.99, 3.35, 5.75, 2.50, 3.01 and 2.61 µg/mL at 1, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 48 and 72 h, with a maximum at 12 h at R² 0.9917. The 36, 48 and 72 h points sit below the first thirty hours as a group (p = 0.006), and all of them stay above the 1.3 µg/mL a plasmid-free WB800 culture gives on the same assay. The team’s own write-up names ten sampling times in one sentence and nine in the next; the ELISA was read at nine, and those nine are what is carried here and on Results.

blocks.en: The DNPH assay on the same samples sits at the floor for the first twelve hours, then reaches 30.9 nmol α-ketobutyrate mL−1 h−1 at 18 h and stays between 10.9 and 18.7 at 24, 30 and 36 h. The 1 h point reads below zero and is an artifact rather than a measurement. Protein peaks at 12 h and activity at 18 h, six hours later. These are the numbers Development and Results show, and they are single samples at each point.

blocks.en: The three-day time course as the team plotted it. Panel C is the one that complicates the harvest argument: concentration falls after 12 hours, but the activity per microgram of protein keeps rising to the end of the run, so the later samples are less protein doing proportionally more. The team’s reading is that ACC deaminase needs to assemble as a multimer and pick up its pyridoxal-5′-phosphate cofactor, which the medium outside the cell is a poor place to do; that is a hypothesis from one run, not a measurement.

blocks.en: The fouling trace is the longest the project has: the pressure the module needs beyond what clean water needs at the same flow rose from 1.9 to 4.4 kPa across the 77 hours, still far from any threshold that would call for cleaning. The photometer’s acceptance gate dropped 81 of 5009 measurement windows over the same run, which is the rejection rate a three-day run produces once the gate is a written specification and not a judgment call.

The economic model assumes a five-hour harvest cycle, and a concentration that peaks at 12 hours and halves after 30 does not support it. That is argued out on Math Model; it is recorded here because this run is where the number came from.

blocks.en: Nobody sells this instrument, so we built it. It reads optical density straight from the flowing culture, with a reference channel split off before the sample so drift in the source divides out. Six cycles, two of them ended by the same class of mistake made twice. Two instruments came out of them, and both are written down stage by stage with the bench tests that gate each stage: the Pro, which is the one in the reactor loop, and the Slim, which is cycle 8.

blocks.en: We used magnetic helping hands, the clip tool that holds parts locked in place and is normally used for soldering, to hold our amber 600 nm LED in line with a purchased paralleling lens. That gives parallel light, which a 2 mm slit then narrows, so only a small part of the beam passes on through the beam splitter to the two lux sensors.

That gives parallel light, which a 2 mm slit then narrows, so only a small part of the beam passes on through the beam splitter to the two lux sensors.

blocks.en: We locked the LED, slit, beam splitter and both lux sensors in position relative to each other and left only the paralleling lens free to move. Fixing everything else made the lens position the single variable.
blocks.text: We locked the LED, slit, beam splitter and both lux sensors in position relative to each other and left only the paralleling lens free to move. Fixing everything else made the lens position the single variable.

blocks.en: With the other components locked down, we shifted the paralleling lens along the axis until the light path steadily illuminated both sensors. Doing that meant nudging the slit and the sensors slightly as well, to bring the path into line. Then we measured the distance between every component and turned the layout into a drawing our drylab hardware team could develop into a CAD model with everything anchored in place.

blocks.en: We had been blanking ReLEAF against growth medium. The Bio-Drop is calibrated on distilled water. The roughly 20% disagreement we had been attributing to our optics was largely a procedural artifact.

blocks.en: The protocol that came out of it is in the user manual, and it goes the other way: blank on the growth medium the run will use, and blank the reference spectrophotometer on the same medium. What matters is not which liquid, it is that both instruments see the same one; the manual names blanking them differently as the commonest cause of disagreement between the two. Changing the sensor settings, the estimator or the path-length factor voids the blank, and an old blank is flagged for the operator, who decides whether to take a new one.

blocks.en: Noise is tight below about 0.4 OD and ragged above about 0.8, so the useful precision is not flat across the range. The rejection rate moved from 42.9% to 14.3% to 0% within one run, and the rejection rule is not yet written down anywhere.
blocks.text: Noise is tight below about 0.4 OD and ragged above about 0.8, so the useful precision is not flat across the range. The rejection rate moved from 42.9% to 14.3% to 0% within one run, and the rejection rule is not yet written down anywhere.

blocks.en: It is written down now, and it has moved on since the run. The specification in the user manual takes four dark readings, turns the source on for 60 ms and takes sixteen lit readings in each window; a reading counts as rejected when it falls more than 5 % below the upper envelope of its burst, and above 50 % rejected the whole measurement is discarded and retaken at once. A second gate sits after it, which refuses a reading whose dispersion or whose jump from the last accepted value is too large and reports the median of the last three accepted values instead. The run’s own three rates belong to the older fourteen-reading burst, where 42.9 % and 14.3 % are exactly six and two readings out of fourteen, so they are a count and not a drift over the run.

blocks.en: Between roughly 240 and 300 hours the scatter grew by an order of magnitude, and over the same hours the reference channel fell from 25.8 lux to 9.3, bottoming at 1.4. The first hypothesis was contamination and it was wrong: the recirculation pump had failed, and swapping it knocked the optical axis. Part of that window is the reactor failing and part of it is us, and the reason we can tell the difference is that the instrument’s own reference channel flagged the window as untrustworthy while it was happening. We would rather put it that way than the way we first wrote it, which was that the photometer detected the pump dying: nobody was rostered to look at the trace daily, and the fault was noticed late.

blocks.en: A separate, earlier feature, a fall from OD 0.93 to 0.72 between 120 and 160 hours, has no attribution at all. The optical channel was healthy through it, so it is not the instrument. Lysis followed by cryptic growth, sporulation and germination, and biofilm sloughing all remain open. The measurement that would have separated fouling from biology is a flush and reblank at the end of the run; it was never done, and once the rig was torn down the chance was gone.

blocks.en: The thing the draft asked for and did not have was the calculation itself: whether the reported OD used the reference channel or only the sample against the blank. The photometer record states it, and it uses both. A blank fixes K, the sample reading divided by the reference reading with medium and no cells in the cell; every live reading is then OD600 = −log<sub>10</sub>[S / (K · R)], so drift in the LED divides out over a multi-week run. The dashboard of this run reported five times that value, and with the factor restored all three snapshots above reproduce on one K of about 9.16.

blocks.en: The ratio flag was half an arithmetic error and half a missing build step. A 90:10 splitter gives a sample-to-reference ratio of 9:1, while the dashboard of this run expected 10:1, so the expectation was set a little high to begin with. The run measured 5.3× to 6.4× throughout, which is low against 9 but inside the band the current app treats as acceptable: the operator enters the split ratio, and the app warns only below half or above double it. What has changed is that the ratio is now something you set, not something you find out afterwards. The assembly guide ends on an alignment step, with the LED turned in its clip under a live reading until sample and reference sit at about 9:1 with neither sensor saturated, and that step is the last thing done before the blank. Had it existed in July, the red flag on the figure above would have been a reading about the culture.

blocks.en: The decision survived into the shipped instrument, and the manual says what it costs: no calibration curve against a reference spectrophotometer is applied, so the optical density the reactor logs is raw output, linear across the working range and not traceable to any reference instrument. It also names where that stops holding. At high cell density the source and the sensor are not linear together, so the top of the range has to be checked with a dilution series and never assumed.

blocks.en: Two single points were excluded, each on objective grounds, and both stay in the figures as open markers. In Test 1, the mg = 37 Bio-Drop reading is a handling error, off the trend of its neighbors. In Test 2, the mg = 5 Bio-Drop reading violates monotonicity, it exceeds the readings both above and below it, which is impossible for an increasing standard. In both cases, the paired ReLEAF reading is on trend.

blocks.en: The raw, uncalibrated ReLEAF output already sits near one-to-one with the reference and tracks the ground-truth mass standard with a residual scatter comparable to the Bio-Drop’s: in Test 1, across 2 to 40 mg, 0.030 OD600 for ReLEAF against 0.031 for the Bio-Drop. A line fit through the raw Test 2 points scatters by an RMSE of 0.011 OD600 about the line of identity, which measures how tight the raw agreement is and is not a correction applied to anything. The SiO<sub>2</sub> calibration we deferred remains available as a future check, but on the strength of the TiO<sub>2</sub> comparison it would only confirm what we already have.

The SiO2 calibration we deferred remains available as a future check, but on the strength of the TiO2 comparison it would only confirm what we already have.

blocks.en: Cycles 7 and 8 are named on the reactor record. Cycle 7, the silicon dioxide calibration deferred above, ran on October 10, 2026: against the reference the current build is one to one to OD 2.5 (slope 0.995), and the numbers are on the photometer page.

blocks.en: Cycle 8, the simplified photometer, has a build. The reasoning that started it was a cost argument: three parts account for most of the price, the flow cuvette earns its own because it is what lets the instrument read the loop live, which left the paralleling lens as the part to remove. What the Slim actually removes is both of them. One 600 nm fiber illuminator feeds two PMMA fibers, one across the culture in the same 2 mm flow cuvette to the sample sensor and one across an empty chamber to the reference sensor, so the splitter goes as well as the lens and the reference channel survives. The electronics are the Pro’s, unchanged: the same Uno Q, the same two GY‑302 sensors on the same two addresses, the same app. The body is a third of the Pro’s filament, 124 g of PLA against 363 g.

blocks.en: It reads, and it does not read on the Pro’s scale. The Slim sits at about a fifth, and one silica standard puts the two together at Pro ≈ 5.57 × Slim − 0.07. That factor rests on one standard on a stable scatterer, with nothing from a culture behind it, so it is a conversion and not yet a validation. The split between the two fibers is also not fixed the way a cube’s is: bump or reseat a fiber and the instrument has to be blanked again. What the Slim costs to build is not written down anywhere; what it displaces is, at about US$370 for the Pro the long run was made on and NT$15 000, roughly US$470, for the Bio-Drop that Pro was checked against. The Pro stays in the reactor loop.

blocks.en: The light plate apparatus (LPA) is a testing apparatus, not part of the control loop. It exists to answer one question: how the wavelength and intensity of applied light affect protectant production in engineered Bacillus subtilis. Four cycles took it from two LEDs on a breadboard to a US$65.52 instrument that lights twenty-four cultures under six defined conditions, with its intensity tiers set in code and each well shielded from its neighbors. The build is written down stage by stage, with its three bench tests and the duty cycle of each tier, in the LPA assembly guide.

blocks.en: Internal-resistance variance is a common problem in cheap single-bulb LEDs: nominally identical parts draw different currents and emit different intensities at the same drive level. As long as that is true, an intensity tier is not a real quantity, and the wavelength comparison is not fair either, since the green and red channels would be running at unknown relative brightness. Ambient light adds an unknown amount of illumination to every tube, and it lands hardest on the low-intensity condition, which is exactly where the separation has to be cleanest.

blocks.en: The approach is to measure the light output of every LED individually and use that to identify units with similar internal resistance. From the matched units we form three groups of four per wavelength, one group per intensity tier, arranged as columns. Because the LEDs within a column are matched, the column can be recalibrated as a unit through straightforward mathematical adjustment, so that every column at a given tier matches every other: that is what turns low, medium and high from labels into reproducible quantities. Coverage was added to block external light, so that the intensity a culture receives is the intensity we set.

blocks.en: Every LED was driven at 5 V and measured individually on a lux meter using a printed sensor fixture, so each reading is taken at the same distance and orientation. Each LED has a tag made of its row and its column, rows A to D running downward and columns 1 to 5 across, so any physical LED can be traced back to its own measurement. The array was then rewired with the matched units grouped into columns.

Sorting those into groups of four by output gives the matched sets the tiers are built from, and the six channels were read again after rewiring.

blocks.en: Sorting by measured output tightens each group considerably: the green low group spans 2.33 to 2.34 and the green mid group 2.35 to 2.37, well inside 1%, and the red groups stay within about 2% each. But the separation between tiers is smaller than we need. Green low to green high is about 4% and red low to red high about 10%. Those gaps are the parts’ own spread after sorting; they are not three distinct light levels. The tiers therefore have to come from the PWM duty cycle rather than from LED selection: matching makes the four LEDs in a column agree with each other, and software sets how bright that column runs.

blocks.en: An outer frame print houses the LED wiring and the perf board, so no electronics sit loose on the bench. Light intensity is varied in code, so a run is defined by a set of values, with nothing for anyone to remember to adjust. Slider prints support the LED holder and the tube holder, so the stack comes apart for rewiring. A tall print positions the test tubes at a fixed position over the array, so the distance between LED and culture is the same every run.

A screwdriver is the only tool the assembly itself needs; the soldering iron is for the four M3 heat-set inserts that take the perf board.

blocks.en: Control runs from an Arduino Uno R4 WiFi. PWM signals from the Arduino drive three MOSFETs, one per intensity tier, and software sets the duty cycle for each tier. The selected intensities are held constant for the duration of a test, so each culture receives a fixed, well-defined dose; three calibrated tiers across two wavelengths give six defined light conditions per run.

blocks.en: The switching stage moved with the build. In cycle 2 the three MOSFETs stood on a breadboard on the bench beside the LED holder; here they sit on the perf board underneath it, with the housing over them. Each tier is one IRLZ44N on its own Arduino pin, and the run sketch writes one value per pin and never changes it again, so the dose a tube receives is set by three numbers in the source.

blocks.en: During our overnight test run, the connection point on the bottom plate broke off. The LPA was on a shaker for the run; the frequency was most likely too high for the printed post. Several wires came undone and had to be resoldered. The white tube holder print also allowed light to leak into neighboring holes, which compromised our data, as the test tubes were receiving light from more than one source.

Neither change has been through a second overnight run on the shaker, so the repair is untested. The white tube holder was replaced with a black one, and its wall thickness increased from two loops to four.

blocks.en: Both repairs are the build now: the assembly guide screws the base plate to the housing from underneath with four #10‑32 screws through the middle of each edge, and prints the tube holder in black at four wall loops. Three bench tests go with it, one after the LEDs are soldered, one after the MOSFETs are wired, and the second one again once the stack is screwed together, so a column that stops answering its MOSFET is caught before a culture is in the tube. None of that is the overnight run, which is still the test this cycle owes.

blocks.en: The last of those is the induction run this track was built for. It has since been done on this apparatus, with the Level 2 strain, and is reported on Results: the signal rises with time under green light but not in an ordered way across intensities, so what the page still waits on is a dose in photon flux and a loading-normalized curve. Earlier faults in the same build are recorded and fixed: one green and red column stopped answering its MOSFET and two ran very weak until the MOSFET was changed, the assembly and disassembly is slow, and the jumper wire on the MOSFET spike sits loose.

blocks.en: Every reading on this track is in lux, which is weighted for human vision and peaks near 555 nm, so the weighting error is not the same size on the green channel as on the red. The dose that matters to the cells is photon flux, in µmol m<sup>−2</sup> s<sup>−1</sup>. The team found this in week 16; until the readings are converted they compare our LEDs with each other and cannot be compared with a published dose.

blocks.en: The final build combines what the three cycles established: LEDs matched by measured output, intensity set by PWM in code, enclosed electronics, a fixed tube position, and a black holder that shields each well. Two changes carried in from cycle 3 define it. The base plate is screwed to the housing at four points instead of two, which spreads the load across the whole edge, and every soldered connection is reinforced. The tube holder is printed in black PLA at four wall loops, with a 1 mm wall between bores, so light from one well stops at the wall instead of reaching its neighbor.

blocks.en: The geometry follows from the question the apparatus answers. Four wells per condition give four replicates; six columns on an 18 mm pitch give two wavelengths at three intensities; and a tube bore of 17 mm over its own LED fixes the distance between source and culture, so a condition is a number in the source and not a position on a bench.

Assembly takes four M6, four #10-32 and four M3 screws, and a screwdriver is the only tool it needs.

blocks.en: A commercial light plate apparatus is an expensive instrument, and the point of this one is that it is not. Six printed parts, one Arduino, three MOSFETs and US$65.52 give twenty-four cultures under six defined conditions, and the whole build is written down stage by stage in the assembly guide, with the duty cycle of each tier and the three bench tests, so another team can reproduce it rather than buy it.

blocks.en: What the apparatus reports is the duty cycle it was set to, which is a stable and repeatable dose but not a photon flux. Putting the tiers in absolute units, and measuring uniformity between wells, is the measurement that would let these conditions be compared with another group’s. That is the next thing this instrument is for.

blocks.en: Prototype 1 was a large opaque tub, 21.1 × 14.1 × 11.4 cm, filled with about 500 mL of ½ MS medium under a foam board cut from sheet and taped black, carrying five agar-containing seed holders. Prototype 2 was a small bought box, 7.5 × 7.5 × 5.3 cm, with holders for the lids and labels on the box lid. Prototype 3 was a tall clear box, 6.5 × 6.5 × 10 cm, with a square black-taped foam board.
blocks.text: Prototype 1 was a large opaque tub, 21.1 × 14.1 × 11.4 cm, filled with about 500 mL of ½ MS medium under a foam board cut from sheet and taped black, carrying five agar-containing seed holders. Prototype 2 was a small bought box, 7.5 × 7.5 × 5.3 cm, with holders for the lids and labels on the box lid. Prototype 3 was a tall clear box, 6.5 × 6.5 × 10 cm, with a square black-taped foam board.

blocks.en: The first box wasted most of what it offered: the board had room for more seed holders than the five we used, the foam was too fragile to reuse, and cutting and taping it was slow and hard to scale up. The depth of the box made the root system difficult to observe, and the black wall made it difficult to tell when the medium went turbid. Prototype 2 leaked from two sites when the box was moved, the joint and the bottom, and black tape over the hole did not stop it; the lid fell into the box unless it was placed at a specific angle. Prototype 3 held opacity and depth together, and then the foam board fitted so tightly that it was hard to reach when the medium was changed, and the box was too narrow for the plants to grow and limited how many we could run in it.

blocks.en: A 1000 µL tip box answered all of it at once. It is 12.8 × 10.1 × 9.5 cm, which does not take up much space and still gives the roots room; it is transparent, so the root system and the turbidity of the medium can both be read off the wall; it survives cleaning and autoclaving, so it is reused; and one board in it takes anything from 5 to 13 holes. Contamination was less frequent than in the two boxes before it.

blocks.en: Labs that grow Arabidopsis in liquid medium improvise the holder: a piece of foam cut to size, a mesh taped over a container, or a fixed plate sitting above a reservoir. Conn and colleagues [6] set out the version we started from, seeds germinated on agar in punched tube lids and then moved onto a board. We did the same, and sized a plate for each of the three box volumes we had on the bench.

blocks.en: The level turned out to be a narrow window. It has to sit just under the board and as high as it can be got: too low and the roots lose contact, too high and the board floods. And it does not stay where it is put. The plants drink and the medium evaporates, so a level that was right at the start of a run is wrong by the end of it.

blocks.en: The foam failed separately. It became soft after it stayed in the water for a long time, and a softened board breaks in the middle of changing the medium.
blocks.text: The foam failed separately. It became soft after it stayed in the water for a long time, and a softened board breaks in the middle of changing the medium.

blocks.en: Two faults with one answer each. Somebody has to watch the reservoir and top it up, and every top-up is a chance for conditions to drift between replicates, which is the variable the board was there to remove in the first place. And a board cut, taped and drilled for one box is not a part another lab can make the same way twice. So print the board, and stop setting a level at all.

blocks.en: Printed in PLA on a standard FDM machine, pontoons hollow at 15 % gyroid infill with a teardrop cross-section that prints without support. A pole at each corner took washers, so the freeboard could be trimmed after printing without reprinting the whole part. A handle went on each side of the board, so the plate could be lifted out to change the medium without anyone touching the seedlings.

Construct map: Pveg promoter, EEBD, RBS0, a SamyQ or csn secretion peptide, the protectant coding sequence, a dashed 6xHis box and B0015, in pSTK-EXP1-sfGFP.
Agarose gel of seven lanes, a ladder and six sample lanes, with bright bands in lanes two, three, four, six and seven.
Agarose gel of twenty-two lanes labelled G1 to G12 and H1 to H10, with strong bands in G2, H2 and H4.

Two predicted RNA secondary structures side by side, wild type at the left and optimized variant at the right, with the RBS region in blue and recoded bases in orange, above a per-base unpaired probability trace comparing the two.
Bar chart of DNPH activity for csn, csn plus PLP, samyQ plus PLP and the WB800 control.
Bar chart of ELISA concentrations for ACCD, LEA and BoPep4 secreted by B. subtilis WB800.

Bioreactor
Bioreactor cycles

Hand drawing of prototype I: a PES hollow fibre membrane at the top, tubing down to a peristaltic pump, a sampling luer valve on the left and a medium reservoir on the right, with orange arrows showing the direction of flow.
Line chart of OD600 against time in hours for two cultures. The flask rises from about 0.2 to 2.5 over twenty-five hours while the bioreactor stays near 0.1 to 0.3 for the whole run.
A single LB agar plate photographed on white cloth, the surface clear and even with no visible colonies.

Hand drawing of prototype II: the hollow fibre membrane at the top, a sampler in the middle of the return line, a peristaltic pump at bottom left and the medium reservoir on a magnetic stirrer at bottom right.

Line chart of OD600 against time in minutes for two cultures at 37 degrees. The bioreactor rises steeply and plateaus near 0.9 after about 150 minutes; the flask reaches a similar level after about 270 minutes.

The reactor running on the bottom shelf of an incubator: a serum bottle on a magnetic stirrer with a luer sampler at its cap, a peristaltic pump, and the printed photometer tower with its flow cuvette, with plants under test on the shelf above.

System schematic of the reactor: reservoir, pump, pressure sensor, hollow-fibre module and pinch valve in a loop, with the sampler and in-line photometer on the loop and the permeate leaving through the membrane toward the plants.
A laptop screen showing four live pressure traces, feed, retentate, permeate and transmembrane, each carrying a heavy periodic oscillation.
A bench with a dissolved-oxygen probe and a pH probe, each in a beaker, both reading on their meters.
A whiteboard worked out as a power tree: mains to twelve volts to five volts, each load assigned to a rail, with the LED driver and an enclosure with a screen and a door sketched beside it.
A projected schematic of prototype II under review at a table, showing membrane, sampler, peristaltic pump, medium reservoir and magnetic stirring, with team members discussing it.

Loop diagram of the first integrated bioreactor. A stirred bottle of B. subtilis feeds a pump, a flow meter and an in-line photometer, then runs up the hollow-fibre membrane past three pressure transducers and back to the bottle through an in-line filter. The protectant pathway leaves the shell side and returns to it, closing on itself with a sampling valve on the loop.

The complete rig running inside an incubator: a 500 millilitre reservoir on a stirrer, the hollow-fibre loop, the pump, an in-line filter, pressure transducers and their boards, with the dashboard displayed on a screen on top of the incubator.

The dashboard at 53 hours 22 minutes: OD600 2.4474 AU, 6,387 samples, flow 371.0 millilitres per minute, cumulative volume 1,132,192.1 millilitres, feed, retentate and permeate pressures near 0.2 bar and a transmembrane pressure of minus 0.0005 bar.

OD600 against time over 116 hours, a grey band from about 4 to 14 hours marking the hours with no data, the smoothed curve rising to about 1.7 by 40 hours, flattening there, then climbing again from about 48 hours to 3.7 at the end.
Two pressure traces over 116 hours: feed pressure near 0.20 to 0.25 bar with frequent downward spikes, and transmembrane pressure flat along zero, with the same grey no-data band from 4 to 14 hours.

Loop diagram: a stirred bottle of B. subtilis with a pH probe in its cap feeds a pump, a flow meter and an in-line photometer, then runs up the hollow-fibre membrane past three pressure transducers and back through a pinch valve, while the protectant pathway leaves the shell side into a separate product bottle.

Three stacked traces over 38 hours from 8 October: OD600 rising to 0.3 then breaking into large oscillations around 1.0, pH falling from 6.55 to 6.22 then jumping and swinging before settling near 6.9, and flow holding near 300 to 390 millilitres per minute, with dashed lines marking where each new recording file starts.

Three grouped bar charts. A, ELISA concentration in micrograms per millilitre at 1, 16, 24 and 40 hours, lumen and shell bars close together in every pair and both between about 4.6 and 8.6. B, DNPH volumetric activity in milliunits per millilitre over the same hours, lumen higher than shell at 1 and 24 hours and the 40-hour lumen bar missing. C, specific activity in units per milligram, the 24-hour lumen bar the tallest at about 9.5.

A scatter plot of change in optical density against standard concentration from zero to about four millimolar with a straight fitted line, and the lumen, shell and 28-hour sample series all clustered at the low end near the origin.

Three stacked dark-background charts over 42 hours from 14 October: OD600 with a raw estimator and a gated reported trace rising together to about 2.7 by 37 hours then jumping off the top of the scale, pH falling from 6.9 to 6.4 by six hours then stepping up to 7.2 after a dose, and feed flow holding near 300 millilitres per minute, each marked with a run-one to run-two seam at 24 hours.

Five stacked charts over about 42 hours. OD600 climbing steadily to 2.7 with dotted lines marking sampling and base additions; feed, shell and retentate pressures holding flat until a pink band at 37 hours where feed jumps from 0.19 to 0.37 bar; lumen pressure drop and flow; mean transmembrane pressure near 0.03 bar with a shaded pulsation band from minus 0.1 to plus 0.17 bar; and feed pressure standard deviation in millibar.
Seven starch-iodide test papers laid out in a row on a paper towel, the speckling that marks peroxide heaviest on the strips at the ends of the row and almost absent on the palest ones.

A chart over about eighteen hours with OD600 on the left axis rising from 0.08 to 1.24 and pH on the right axis falling from 6.9 to 6.4. The OD curve climbs steeply to six hours and then flattens into a slow rise at the same time as the pH curve passes 6.5.

Loop diagram of the final bioreactor. A stirred bottle of B. subtilis with a pH probe feeds a pump, a flow meter and an in-line photometer, then runs up the hollow-fibre membrane past three pressure transducers and back through a pinch valve and a feeding Luer valve, where a second pump adds KOH or external feed. A shell Luer valve takes the protectant pathway out of the membrane into its own output bottle.

Two stacked charts over eighty hours. OD600 rises from 0.18 through a steep climb between two and nine hours to 1.4, then a long slow rise to 3.28 at the end. Below it pH traces a sawtooth, drifting down from 7.0 and jumping back up at about 24, 49 and 73 hours, never falling below 6.3.

Three stacked charts across about 160 seconds, shaded into normal operation, prep, sampling with the pinch valve closed, release and back to normal. Feed pressure steps from 0.16 to 0.24 bar while the pinch valve is closed and the permeate pressure drops to near zero when the shell valve opens; mean transmembrane pressure rises from 0.03 to 0.16 bar with its pulsation band shifting entirely above zero; lumen flow dips from 305 to about 283 millilitres per minute.
A white 3D-printed pinch valve on a wooden bench, a clear silicone tube running through a slot in its body and a black STS3215 serial servo bolted into the frame beside a printed cam.
A white 3D-printed housing holding a Luer valve with a printed gear on its handle, driven by a black serial servo, with tubing entering from both sides.

Three bar charts of the shell permeate at 1, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 48 and 72 hours. A, ELISA concentration peaking at 6.5 micrograms per millilitre at 12 hours and falling to 2.6 by 72. B, DNPH volumetric activity, nothing at 1 hour, a step up at 18 hours and a plateau after it. C, specific activity, near zero for the first twelve hours and then climbing to its highest value at 72 hours.
Photometer
Photometer cycles

A bench alignment rig: blue magnetic helping-hands arms holding a beam splitter in an aluminium housing and a cuvette in line, a steel rule and a digital caliper laid under them, with a breadboard and the LED on the left.
The first photometer build: every optical component on a horizontal printed rail, with the flow cuvette in the middle of the beam and tubing entering from both sides.
The vertical photometer tower running in a darkened enclosure, the LED glowing at the top of the printed column with the flow cuvette below it and tubing running out to the loop.
The photometer tilted about ten degrees on a printed wedge, tubing entering the flow cuvette at the base of the column.

A dashboard screenshot from 19 July at 19:06 showing an optical density reading roughly four times the benchtop value for the same sample, with the sample to reference ratio reading 8.18 times against a design figure of about ten to one.

The photometer dashboard ten days and four hours into the long run, showing the optical density trace with a dip and recovery around 150 hours, the point count, and the sample to reference ratio flagged in red at 4.64 times.
CAD render of the final photometer: a tall printed column with snap-in covers over the light path, a wide base and a wedge under the body that sets the tilt.
The calibration being run on the bench: the photometer in a recirculating loop with a stirred reservoir and the benchtop instrument beside it, with values being written down by hand.
Scatter plot of ReLEAF OD600 against BioDrop OD600 for the second calibration test, twenty points lying close to the dashed line of identity, annotated slope 0.942 and R squared 0.9997.
LPA
Light plate apparatus cycles
A printed black circular fixture on a table holding one green LED at its centre, wired out to a bench supply, used to measure each LED at the same distance and orientation.

The finished light plate apparatus: a printed white tube holder with twenty-four wells lit in alternating green and red sitting in a black enclosure, one transparent tube glowing green, with the Arduino on the bench beside it.

A grey printed bottom plate with a cone-shaped base; fingers hold the snapped-off cylindrical post just above it, a screw through its top, with the perf board, three MOSFETs and dust on the plate behind.

The finished light plate apparatus on a wooden desk: a black printed tube holder with twenty-four round bores in a four by six grid, seated on top of a black printed housing with a slider tab along its side and a ribbon of coloured wires leaving the right-hand end.

The light plate apparatus running inside an incubator on a shaker: capped culture tubes standing in the tube holder glow green and red from the LEDs beneath them, with the Arduino and tagged wires on the tray beside it.

Hydroponics cycles
Prototype 1: a black opaque tub, 21.1 by 14.1 by 11.4 centimetres, with its black foam board.
Prototype 2: a small blue box with a red holder and a clear lid, 7.5 by 7.5 by 5.3 centimetres.
Prototype 3: a tall clear box, 6.5 by 6.5 by 10 centimetres, with a black foam board inside.
Three black perforated foam boards leaning against a wall on a bench, hand-labelled in red tape with 1.5 L, 2 L and 300 mL.
Prototype 4: a clear 1000 microlitre tip box, 12.8 by 10.1 by 9.5 centimetres, with a white foam board floating inside.

The first printed floating plate on a dark table: a white slab perforated with a grid of holes over a closed hollow frame, with a threaded pole and a washer stack rising from each of the four corners.
Students at a bench assembling a perforated white float plate for the hydroponic boxes.

Render of the floating plate from its CAD, cut across the outer row of seed holders. A dark slab is carried by a pontoon along each long side; inside each pontoon is a violet sealed chamber that closes to a point. Brown seed holders sit in the bores and a grey handle stands at the far end.
The clear tip box with a black 3D-printed float board inside.

The clear hydroponic box sitting inside the black light-blocking box.
